**Scottish Government — 2,000 consultation replies, read by machine and checked by people (2025)**

In 2025 the Scottish Government consulted the public on how to regulate non-surgical cosmetic procedures — lip fillers, laser hair removal and the like. More than 2,000 people replied across six open-text questions. Reading every reply, grouping what people said and working out which themes dominate is exactly the kind of document work that swallows analyst weeks.

Instead, officials ran the responses through Consult, a tool built by the UK government's Incubator for AI. The brief was not "summarise this". It was specific: find the themes in the replies, assign every individual response to a theme, and show an analyst which response sits where, so the grouping could be inspected rather than taken on trust.

Because it was the first live use, the Scottish Government's own experts also analysed every response by hand. In the majority of cases they agreed with the choices the tool had made, and where they differed the effect on how the themes ranked overall was reported as negligible. The government said that across roughly 500 consultations a year the approach could remove around 75,000 days of manual analysis, worth about £20m in staff time — with human reviewers still signing off the themes.

Your version is smaller: one 30-page report, not 2,000 replies. The pattern transfers exactly. Give the assistant a real brief — audience, length, focus, format — let it do the reading, then skim its output against the source before you act on it. That check is not a formality; it is what makes the time you saved defensible.

**UK Department for Transport — the spreadsheet nobody re-checked (2012)**

In 2012 the Department for Transport ran the competition to award the InterCity West Coast rail franchise. Part of the decision rested on a financial model in a spreadsheet, used to work out how much risk capital each bidder had to put up. Weeks after naming a winner, the department cancelled the entire competition: the model contained errors, with inflation and risk adjustments applied inconsistently between bids.

The National Audit Office found the most instructive detail. The tool "had been designed to inform internal discussions and received no extra quality assurance once the Department decided to use it to calculate the loan, a key commercial decision". Nothing was wrong with building a rough model to inform a discussion. What went wrong was promoting that model to the basis of a public decision without anyone re-checking it.

The NAO identified £1.9m of staff and adviser costs, £2.7m of legal costs and £4.3m spent on external reviews, and said the full cost to the taxpayer was unknown but likely to be significant. No AI appears anywhere in this story — which is rather the point. The failure mode is older than these tools: a figure that looked authoritative because it came out of a spreadsheet.

That is why this lesson is firm about its two rules. An assistant will write you a working formula and spot real patterns in a pasted table, and it will also type a plausible total that no formula ever computed. Let the spreadsheet do the arithmetic, treat any number the AI types as a claim rather than a fact, and verify anything heading for a client, a board or a regulator.

**NASA — the warning that lived at the bottom of a slide (2003)**

While the shuttle Columbia was in orbit in January 2003, engineers were assessing whether foam debris that struck the wing at launch had caused serious damage. Their analysis reached managers the way most analysis reaches managers: as presentation slides.

The key slide was headed "Review Of Test Data Indicates Conservatism for Tile Penetration" — a title that reads like reassurance. Beneath it, in a nest of ever-smaller sub-bullets, sat the point that mattered: the piece of foam that had actually hit the orbiter was far larger than anything the test data behind the damage model covered. The most important statement on the slide was the least prominent thing on it.

The Columbia Accident Investigation Board, reporting later that year, wrote that it "was surprised to receive similar presentation slides from NASA officials in place of technical reports", and described "the endemic use of PowerPoint briefing slides instead of technical papers" as an illustration of problematic methods of technical communication. Seven astronauts died and the board found many causes; the slides are one thread, and they are the thread that anyone who builds decks can act on.

Nothing in your working week carries stakes remotely like that. The habit still transfers. When you ask an assistant for per-slide headlines, insist each one states the slide's message rather than its topic, read the ten headlines in sequence to check you can hear the whole argument, and make sure the uncomfortable caveat has become a headline of its own rather than the smallest line on a crowded slide.

**Gold Coast Hospital and Health Service — 7,499 appointments written up by a listening assistant (2024)**

For 16 weeks from July 2024, this Queensland health service gave 100 clinicians across 19 outpatient specialties an ambient scribe: a tool that listens to the consultation and drafts the clinical note from it. Unscripted, interrupted, jargon-heavy conversation goes in; a structured record comes out. It is the same move as handing a 90-minute meeting transcript to an assistant and asking for minutes.

The published evaluation was warm about structure. Reviewers scored the AI-drafted notes higher overall than the clinician-written ones — 37.06 against 34.6 out of 40 on a standard note-quality scale — praising thorough, well-organised documentation, and 84% of clinicians said their efficiency improved.

The same evaluation is where the caution lives. Forty-seven per cent of staff reported the tool stating clinical detail that had not been said — medications, allergies, measurements — and accuracy was its weakest dimension, while 58% of drafts were accepted with no edit at all. Strong drafting, thin reviewing: the risk sits in the gap between those two numbers, which is why the evaluation stressed that clinician review stays essential.

This lesson has you feed an assistant your messiest inputs: transcripts, a 47-message thread, a photo of a whiteboard. Expect what those clinicians got — better structure than you would have produced by hand, plus the occasional confident detail nobody said. So brief it to flag anything ambiguous instead of guessing, and read the minutes and action table against your own memory of the room before they go anywhere official.

**U.S. General Services Administration — a "model garden", not a winner (2025)**

In August 2025 the General Services Administration, the agency that buys and runs shared services for the US federal government, launched USAi: an internal platform giving federal staff access to assistants from several vendors — Anthropic, Google, Meta and OpenAI among them — through one government-run front door.

What it pointedly did not do was crown a best assistant. Teams can put the same task through different models and compare them on usability, speed, cost and the other criteria that matter to their own work. GSA's chief information officer described the goal as a "model garden — a portfolio of models that our users can choose from, because they all have different strengths and weaknesses".

The second decision is as instructive as the first. The models sit inside an approved government environment rather than on the open web, so staff working with official material had a sanctioned place to do it. Which assistant fits the task, and which assistant is allowed to see this material, were treated as two separate questions — and both were answered before anyone typed a prompt.

You will never run a procurement, but you face those same two questions each time you open an assistant. Take a brief you genuinely use — a summary-spec, a deck outline, an action table pulled from a transcript — and run it through whichever assistants your work allows. That is your own small model garden, and it tells you more than any league table, because it stays valid when next year's versions land.
